title: Kissing Cousins:  A History of Marrying Family
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and science of marrying relatives, focusing on cousin marriage and incest taboos. They cover animal inbreeding avoidance, the Westermarck effect and genetic sexual attraction, royal and elite sibling marriages (Cleopatra, Habsburgs, Zoroastrian xwaedodah), cousin marriage rates from agriculture onward, Robin Fox's estimate, China's cousin marriage law, Joseph Henrich's Church-ban hypothesis, US state laws (Kansas 1858), the du Pont and Rothschild families, the health risks of recessive genes, famous cousin marriages (Poe, Jesse James, Einstein), and marriage customs such as milk kinship, levirate marriage, and baby marriage. The episode ends with listener mail about the phrase "gave up" for adoption.
topics: Joseph Henrich Catholic Church marriage rule

segments.title: Opening banter and cousins
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about their families and how few cousins they have, then introduce the idea that marrying cousins is accepted in much of the world while sibling and parent-child unions are taboo nearly everywhere.

segments.title: Animal inbreeding avoidance and the origin of the taboo
segments.summary: They discuss animals avoiding interbreeding based on inbreeding depression, and two theories for the human taboo: innate aversion versus learned rules. They describe Jonathan Haidt's moral scenario about siblings having consensual sex.

segments.title: Westermarck effect and genetic sexual attraction
segments.summary: They explain the Westermarck effect, where people raised together are not sexually attracted later, and its extension to non-blood relatives. They describe genetic sexual attraction among reunited adoptees and a UK council pamphlet on the subject.

segments.title: Elite sibling marriage through history
segments.summary: They discuss religious myths of sibling unions, the fact that elites rather than commoners practiced royal incest for power consolidation, Cleopatra's marriages, a Roman Egyptian census showing sibling marriages, and the Zoroastrian xwaedodah ritual in Persia.

segments.title: Cousin marriage history and agriculture
segments.summary: A recent DNA study of nearly 1,800 ancient humans found cousin marriage was rare, about three percent, and became more common after agriculture. Robin Fox estimated that a large share of historical marriages were second cousin or closer because people courted within a short walking distance.

segments.title: China, the Catholic Church ban, and Henrich's theory
segments.summary: They cover China's history of first-cousin marriage and the 1980s PRC marriage law banning it, the Catholic Church's third-cousin rule around 506 CE, and Joseph Henrich's hypothesis that the rule helped create individualism and trust in larger societies.
topics: Joseph Henrich Catholic Church marriage rule

segments.title: Habsburgs, du Ponts, Rothschilds and US laws
segments.summary: They discuss the Habsburg jaw and infant mortality, and how families like the du Ponts and Rothschilds kept wealth in the family by marrying cousins. They then cover US state incest laws beginning with Kansas in 1858 and current US first-cousin bans.

segments.title: Health risks, famous cousin marriages and customs
segments.summary: They explain that recessive genetic disorders are the main risk of related unions but remain rare, and mention a Pakistani study on population versus individual effects. They cover famous cousin marriages (Poe, Jesse James, Einstein) and customs like milk kinship, levirate marriage, and baby marriage.

segments.title: Listener mail: adoption language
segments.summary: A listener named Frank writes that the phrase 'gave up' for adoption is frowned upon in the adoption community, and that 'adoption plan' is preferred. The hosts agree.
